rationale: A voice drives a pencil to write for a person's hand, which is speech-driven writing assistance, not a lesson-presenting, answer-grading computer system like PLATO I.
Ship on gyro control while figures are checked on an electronic calculator: onboard calculation for navigation, but no computer performing orbital maneuvers or steering.
A 'thinkwriter' in capable hands points to thought-to-text, but the quote says nothing about decoding brain signals into sentences.
A master computer at a gate recording the identities of everyone passing matches machine-checked access, but there is no card or token read by the machine.
Loading tapes into a projector to educate someone is playback of stored content, not querying a large collection for matching items.
A tracer encodes a description to search a file for any resembling person: matching a person against stored records, but via descriptive coding rather than camera face matching.
Units that break down signal the nearest unit and others respond: coordinated robot population, but peer-to-peer rather than a central computer directing warehouse robots.
Colored filaments in a hull display the ship's functioning, a status display, not live positions of tracked objects from radar on a console.
Ship functions including crew care relegated to robots and automatic machinery matches automatic running of a station, but Skylab's computer only handled attitude and pointing.
A slab changes colour and shows new lines of characters on command: a rewritable surface, though the mechanism is unspecified and it's more like a color screen than e-paper.
Cruiser-finders tuned to detect air-city motors are detectors only; no computer plotting live positions on a display.
A computer being conditioned by fiction until it cannot tell real from unreal is data corruption of a mind, loosely akin to tampering, not network intrusion.
Statistical predictions not prophecies hints at predictive analysis, but nothing about a computer analysing battle data or planning operations.
A spoken command to a vocoder to supply a recording of a conversation is a voice command, though the vocoder's recognition mechanism is unstated.
Touching numbered knobs to order dinner on a mirror in the kitchen is touch-panel input; the key mechanism of selecting by touch matches, with knobs rather than a screen and an ordering context.
A radio contact exchange asking who is speaking has no computing for orbits or course steering.
Face recognition would need a huge Brain, pointing at computer face recognition as a hard problem, but describes no working system.
Lensmen condensing a picture in a tactical tank is a tactical display, but operated by telepathic beings rather than radar-fed computer consoles.
Currents from a helmet fed into the base of the skull to create experience matches feeding senses a simulated world, but via direct neural input rather than a display headset.
Mind reading by staring into eyes is telepathic, with no machine reading images from brain signals.
A sensor-wired glove where touching fingers together starts music is gesture control read by wiring, though without a screen or the PLATO touch panel.
Someone questioning dreams is vague and names no device reading brain activity.
A device linked to the mind responsive to thought matches thought control of a machine, but the link is described as invisible nerve-like tracts with no signals read from an implant.
A Masonic pass over a silvery object to make it loosen bonds is a contactless gesture trigger, loosely like gesture control.
A metal ident card tripping electronic relays gets him past robot guards: a machine-read identity card granting access, though the PLATO-like dining hall context differs.
A giant computer designed largely via circuit equations from a simpler prototype machine matches computers helping design computers; the context is circuit design rather than car parts.
A crystalline plastic keyed to the wearer's EEG pattern acts as an access token read by machines, but uses brain-wave resonance rather than encoded data.
Machines each controlled by a computer replicating a human mind describes automated plant control, but the autonomous maintenance and lights-out operation aren't stated.
The ship's computer did the work without error: onboard computing for the voyage, but the quote does not say it calculates or performs maneuvers.
Ned answering quickly like a rehearsed straight man says nothing about a machine retrieving records.
Feeding a new course into computers and the vessel shifting in response matches an onboard computer executing a maneuver; the key mechanism matches, with the context fictional.
Fingertip whorls triggering a light-switch mechanism is fingerprint-based access, though it's automatic recognition without any computer analysis or stored models.
Spaceships that run themselves with completely automatic controls matches automated flight, but without computed orbits or maneuvers.
Two men sharing a dream world created by one with feedback is a shared virtual world, though MUD1 is a text game over a network and the mechanism differs.
Classroom hearing lessons through a megaphone with a student plugging in is audio instruction equipment, loosely related to a teaching computer.
A line of spoken editorial choice with no machine transcribing speech.
Energy fingers that do anything at mental command fits thought control of devices, but no signal reading from a brain is described.
Controlling a robot from sketchy light representations on a teleview matches remote operation by display, though Goertz manipulators used direct mechanical linkage.
Hilton releases thought-controlled blocks on the ship's controls: thought control of machinery, with no mechanism of reading brain signals.
A circuit linking every machine in the city to a master control for problems is networked computers, but no remote terminals or telephone links are described.
Predicting what a man will do seconds ahead from muscular and nervous preparation is an anticipatory sensing idea, not decoding viewed images from brain signals.
A spoken request to a government information desk expecting a retrieved answer is query-based retrieval; the voice interface differs from Dialog's typed searches.
Standing in a convincingly sensed meadow matches immersive simulated worlds; no headset or apparatus described.
A Boston terrier that turns out not to be alive is an artificial pet, but the passage shows a deception rather than a toy dog.
Walking down rows to blast something is unrelated to a crime database; only loosely hints at tracking.
A mechanical voice stating a request is synthetic speech, but it lacks any mechanism like a talking calculator or reading machine.
Adapting something to an electronic calculator's mechanical aspects mentions calculators but not a pocket-size portable device.
A helmet worn so a man thinks into it and becomes an extension matches thought control of a machine, but no implant or cursor control is mentioned.
Rebuilding the computer Lulu into Margie mentions a computer without any navigation or orbital function.
Ferroelectric computer brains considered and acted: control by computers, but no specific navigation function.
A cart delivering coffee suggests automatic service but nothing about recognising spoken commands.
Placing palms on a plate glowing in the table to be identified matches machine-read biometrics; palm rather than fingerprint, and no computer analysis.
A course record card slipped into a machine that automatically records the mark is an automated test grading function, without presenting lessons.
Whirring computers and calculators behind a human achievement is too generic for an onboard guidance computer.
A nerve-focused device reconstructing speech via a neuronic brain is silent speech decoding, inverse of synthesis, so only loosely related.
Dim figures moving in an illuminated space hint at thought display but no decoding of brain signals into text.
A weather robot on the planet's dark side sending a signal matches unmanned probes returning data, though Luna 1 was a flyby.

Living through a movie with full sensory participation matches immersive VR in function, but the mechanism is unstated.
Resurrecting old summaries and re-running them for investigation is database-based detective work, loosely like NCIC.
Electrodes picking up sub-vocalization nerve impulses and a computer turning them into words matches decoding neural signals to speech, though from peripheral nerves, not brain.
A helmet making the pilot part of the ship is a neural link in fiction, not a prosthesis stimulating nerves for hearing.
Mechanical disks carrying common units of enunciation produce a robot's speech, a synthesized-speech idea, but mechanical and not electronic.
A tubular steel war machine with a blank mind is a robot soldier, but not an autonomous mine.
Mail-sorting robots scanning addresses photoelectrically match optical reading for mail sorting; context differs in being robots.
A machine answering only the user's questions matches question answering, but nothing on natural-language parsing or online access.
Operating a compact computer to align the ship's velocity vector matches onboard computer maneuvering; the stars-visible context is different.
Giant computers solving problems too technical for humans is generic computing, not guidance computations.
A computer replying in text about human limitations is a conversational machine; nothing on pattern matching.
A master machine to which controlled machines respond through a nervous-system-like control network matches a central computer directing many units.
A machine that records impressions affecting its subsequent actions matches learning from experience; SNARC learned via reinforcement in a maze, so the context differs.
A plastic front responsive to a visual projector letting any value appear on a card is a rewritable surface, but projector-driven rather than electronic.
Robots sensitive enough to detect brain discharges, a machine reading brain activity; no reconstruction of images.
Dictating into a microphone of a typing machine which transcribes words matches speech transcription; the human editing step differs.
A voice from a girder telling her something is forbidden is a machine voice, with no description of synthesis.
A huge three-dimensional chart of a star system is a static map, not live tracking from radar.
A machine beating a master chess player for four hours matches a chess computer, but not the consumer product.
A mechanism that grows richer in associations from fed material and learns matches machine learning; SNARC is a reinforcement maze learner.
A current transformed into a visible actual representation of the thinker's thoughts is thought display, but the mechanism is fanciful.
A machine chewing on an entry and answering INSUFFICIENT DATA is a question-answering computer, though not in natural English.
An android teacher assuming a lecture posture is a robot teacher, not a computer lesson system.
Feeding variations of the French from MCO into the Machine's memory matches a chess computer using stored openings; not a consumer device.
A thing revealed to be an automaton fits humanoid robots loosely; no walking, speaking or voice control.
A skull-attached bone-conduction speaker is body-worn audio, not a cochlear implant.
Talking into a machine and words appearing on paper matches dictation; though mechanism unstated.
A mechanical educator used on a creature is a teaching/knowledge-transfer device, not reading images from a brain.
A thumb pressed on a sensor plate in a box is fingerprint sensing, with no automated analysis mentioned.
Feeding libraries into a computer's memory and setting problems, loosely storage; no retrieval of matching records.
A director voices a demand for a summary and gets it printed within a moment; query retrieval from data with a voice interface.
Magnetic readers scanning tags in cars and transmitting identities to headquarters is tracking by machine reading, but of cars rather than offenders.
Radar data fed into a calculator while the ship is set on automatic: computer-aided tracking of a body; no orbital burn.
Computers hooked into central banks storing information on everybody matches networked terminals and databases, with no phone lines or remote consoles.
A retinal pattern checked against an identity center's records matches retinal recognition; the scanner is not described.
Machines running the machines matches automated plants, without any mention of a lights-out factory.
A psychomat that was a fad like the ouija board suggests thought-divination but no text decoding.
A machine whose size is due to its computation section is too generic for medical diagnosis.
A Marriage Integrator matching men and women is computer matchmaking; unconscious desires differ from questionnaire matching.
Thousand Barton tapes answering all questions in his voice is a conversational responder, but prerecorded and not constructed from user input.
Units keyed to operate by the owner's thought pattern is machine access by personal identity; the biometric is brain patterns, not an encoded card.
Being thrust into the picture and situation with challenge and response matches immersive simulation, though psychological.
Taking language lessons en route suggests automated instruction, but no machine described.
Experiments with a thought-spectrum hint at thought visualisation but no device is described.
Keys clacking on their own as a machine responds to the writer is a text-replying machine; unrelated to pattern matching.
Mobile repair units dispatched on scan failure and an emergency prompt match a computer-run station's operations, beyond Skylab's attitude control.
Converting psychons into a current actuating a vocal apparatus to speak is machine speech generation, but the mechanism is fanciful.
A computer selecting a contract partner from available women by traits in thirty-two seconds matches computer matchmaking; the mandatory State context differs.
A Brain actuated by the user's thoughts, a thought-controlled machine, but a weapon in fiction with no cursor or interface.
A wall rack holding illuminated, magnified book sheets read reclining matches a backlit electronic book reader, without being handheld or digital.
Four receptionists with no machine function at all.
A helmet detecting motor impulses from the brain and broadcasting them to guide a robot matches brain-controlled devices; non-invasive here and the robot is a body.
Holding a disk to the left eye for twenty seconds to record the eyeprint matches eye-based identification; the capture mechanism differs from the retinal scanner.
A pilot receiving orbits and courses from a computer matches computed navigation, but is a philosophical remark.
Personnel records bollixed hints at tampered records but no break-in.
Living organisms processing information in parallel like automata matches neural network ideas; nothing about training or recognition.
A sonotyper buried on a shelf is a transcribing device in passing, with no function described.
A wall scanning device checking people against a store of registered images and data matches face recognition against stored images.
A poetry machine emitting text matches machine-generated writing, though poetry rather than weather forecasts.
A borrowed master computer like a dial-covered refrigerator is a big computer, no guidance.
A desk of clicking tabulators summarising city details is data-processing machinery, not a CRT display.
The Marriage Integrator matched Julia with an ordinary mortal, computer matchmaking, with little detail.
Putting in a new circuit describing a repair problem, crystalline neurosis, is loosely manipulating a computer with false input, not intrusion.
A robot scanning his features to identify him matches face recognition; context is fictional.
Machines rejecting the card whenever that number is presented for food or clothes matches card-based machine checking of identity and access.
Telling a machine the date by microphone is speech input, not conversation.
An electronic cross-index for a Library matches computerised information lookup in function, mechanism vague.
Recorded words electronically assembled to answer many questions matches concatenative speech output; not a calculator.
A helmet on a man used to find the whereabouts of someone is a questioning device, not an image reconstruction.
A thinkwriter in capable hands to control human history, a machine writing as the user directs, with no speech or dictation mechanism.
Everything automatic unless a robot or computer calls for help matches a computer running a station's systems; the context is a ship.
Game theory applying to chess because programming can bluff is a remark on programmed chess, no machine product.
Synaptic cell-clusters reminding him of the human brain evokes neural machinery, but no learning or recognition.
I-P computers dismissing a math feat is calculation, with no spacecraft or onboard role.
A midgit-idgit checking colonists' personal attributes is a computer looking up records, with little specified.
An Operations tank seven hundred feet in diameter is a large tactical display, but no live tracking.
Taped data arriving by radio facsimile from an Earth computer is remote data link, a network function; no terminals.
Lantrel slides a form into a thinkwriter and watches it type is a machine that writes for him, with no brain signals decoded.
Feeding coordinates into a machine and mental figures hint at lookups but with no retrieval from records.
Temple awakes into dreams he knows are dreams: an experienced simulated reality, with no device described.
The owner's brain wavelength as the controlling factor is a biometric key that grants access; brain wave rather than card data.
Ohm craving light like a human craves food is a robot with life-like needs, a stretch from a toy dog.
